title: 2 Kings 23:31–37
context: Jehoahaz reigns three months before Pharaoh Necoh removes him and imposes tribute. Necoh installs Eliakim, renamed Jehoiakim, who taxes the people to pay Egypt and does evil like his fathers.

verses.text: Jehoahaz was twenty-three years old when he began to reign; and he reigned three months in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Hamutal the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah.
verses.arminianNotes: Jehoahaz begins to reign at twenty-three and reigns three months. Arminian readers see a brief reign that quickly ends under foreign power.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the short reign as a sign of Judah’s instability. Readers in this tradition note that Jeremiah 22:10–12 is often understood as referring to this king under the name Shallum.

verses.text: He did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, according to all that his fathers had done.
verses.arminianNotes: Jehoahaz “did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, according to all that his fathers had done.” Arminian readers see a son who did not follow Josiah’s example.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the return to evil after Josiah’s reforms. The verdict shows that reform in one generation does not guarantee faithfulness in the next.

verses.text: Pharaoh Necoh put him in bonds at Riblah in the land of Hamath, that he might not reign in Jerusalem; and put the land to a tribute of one hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold.
verses.arminianNotes: Pharaoh Necoh imprisons Jehoahaz at Riblah and imposes tribute. Arminian readers see Judah falling under foreign control as a consequence of its turning from God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s judgment working through Egypt’s power. The tribute of silver and gold marks Judah’s new subordinate status.

verses.text: Pharaoh Necoh made Eliakim the son of Josiah king in the place of Josiah his father, and changed his name to Jehoiakim; but he took Jehoahaz away, and he came to Egypt and died there.
verses.arminianNotes: Necoh makes Eliakim king, renames him Jehoiakim, and takes Jehoahaz to Egypt, where he dies. Arminian readers see Judah’s kings now appointed and named by a foreign ruler.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the loss of independence. The renaming signals Pharaoh’s authority over Judah’s throne, a further step in the loss of the kingdom’s independence.

verses.text: Jehoiakim gave the silver and the gold to Pharaoh; but he taxed the land to give the money according to the commandment of Pharaoh. He exacted the silver and the gold of the people of the land, from everyone according to his assessment, to give it to Pharaoh Necoh.
verses.arminianNotes: Jehoiakim taxes the land to pay Pharaoh, exacting silver and gold from the people. Arminian readers see the burden of foreign domination falling on ordinary people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the people bearing the cost of the kingdom’s decline. Readers in this tradition note that Jeremiah 22:13–19 criticizes Jehoiakim’s reign, though not this tax specifically.

verses.text: Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Zebidah the daughter of Pedaiah of Rumah.
verses.arminianNotes: Jehoiakim begins to reign at twenty-five and reigns eleven years. Arminian readers see a longer reign that will continue Judah’s slide toward exile.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the regnal details introducing another king of the final years. The narrative continues the pattern of decline after Josiah.

verses.text: He did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, according to all that his fathers had done.
verses.arminianNotes: Jehoiakim “did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, according to all that his fathers had done.” Arminian readers see another king choosing unfaithfulness despite Josiah’s example.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the return to evil confirming the narrator’s explanation in 23:26–27. Readers in this tradition see Judah moving toward the judgment already announced.
